messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 5000, E 2000 is [2000, 5000]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-12, 12]}, visible_on: 'C-102'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'DESIGN:SR-100', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('18+00@12R', 'PC-1'; BC-1 and EC-1 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('30+00@12R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Draft the design model for ELM-AVE. The alignment begins at N 3000.00, E 1000.00, station 10+00. It runs S 80°00'00" E for 800.00 ft to PI-1, where it deflects 40°00'00" to the left on a 500 ft radius curve; then 700.00 ft to PI-2, where it deflects 25°00'00" to the right on a 700 ft radius curve; then 600.00 ft to its end. It has two 11 ft lanes and 5 ft shoulders. Draw the centerline on align_MAIN, the edges of pavement on rd_EP and the outside edges of shoulder on rd_ES, and label the stations every 100 ft.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

messages.reasoning:
Let me start by understanding the task and then work through it step by step.

First, I need to understand what's in the document. Let me check the document state.

The task is to draft a roadway design for ELM-AVE with:
- Start point: N 3000.00, E 1000.00 (which in RoadDraft coordinates is [1000.00, 3000.00]), station 10+00
- First leg: S 80°00'00" E for 800.00 ft to PI-1
- At PI-1: deflects 40°00'00" left on a 500 ft radius curve
- Then: 700.00 ft to PI-2
- At PI-2: deflects 25°00'00" right on a 700 ft radius curve
- Then: 600.00 ft to end
- Two 11 ft lanes = 22 ft total pavement width
- 5 ft shoulders on each side = 10 ft total shoulder width
- So edge of pavement offsets are [-11, 11] from centerline (left/right)
- Outside edges of shoulder offsets are [-16, 16] from centerline (-11 - 5 = -16, 11 + 5 = 16)

Wait, let me reconsider the coordinate system. The task says "N 3000.00, E 1000.00" but also says that in this system, N 5000, E 2000 is [2000, 5000]. So x=easting, y=northing. That means [1000, 3000] is the starting point.

Now let me plan my workflow:
1. Get document state to see what's there
2. Create layers align_MAIN, rd_EP, rd_ES if they don't exist
3. Create the alignment using create_alignment with legs


4. Draw the alignment geometry using draw_alignment on the appropriate layer
5. Generate offset lines for pavement edges at ±11 ft and shoulder boundaries at ±16 ft
6. Annotate stations along the entire route at 100-ft intervals
7. Review the completed model

I'll execute these steps systematically, starting with checking the current document state.

Good, I can see the document has layers already created (align_MAIN, rd_EP, rd_ES) but no alignments yet. Let me create the alignment for ELM-AVE based on the description provided.

The alignment:
- Starts at N 3000.00, E 1000.00 (which is [1000.00, 3000.00] in RoadDraft format)
- Station: 10+00 = 1000 ft
- Leg 1: S 80°00'00" E for 800.00 ft to PI-1
- At PI-1: deflects 40°00'00" left on 500 ft radius curve for 700.00 ft to PI-2
- At PI-2: deflects 25°00'00" right on 700 ft radius curve for 600.00 ft to END

Let me compute the coordinates step by step:

Starting point: [1000.00, 3000.00] at station 1000 ft

Leg 1: S 80°00'00" E for 800 ft
- Bearing "S 80°00'00" E" means from South, 80° toward East
- This is an azimuth of 180 - 80 = 100° clockwise from North
- dx = 800 * sin(100°) = 800 * 0.9848 = 787.85
- dy = 800 * cos(100°) = 800 * (-0.1736) = -138.90
- PI-1: [1000 + 787.85, 3000 - 138.90] = [1787.85, 2861.10]


- Station at PI-1: 1000 + 800 = 1800 ft

Leg 2 involves a left deflection at PI-1 with a 500 ft radius. Since we're turning left and coming into PI-1 from the first leg, I need to determine the new direction. The previous bearing was S 80° E (azimuth 100°), and a left turn of 40° gives us a new azimuth of 60°.

Converting this to a quadrant bearing: an azimuth of 60° corresponds to N 60° E. Over the 700 ft curve length, the tangent distance is T = R * tan(Δ/2) = 500 * tan(20°) ≈ 181.99 ft. Using the standard road geometry formulas, I can find the curve's geometry parameters including its central angle and other key dimensions.

For the second leg starting after the curve, I need to calculate where PI-2 ends up. The deflection angle there turns right 25°, giving an azimuth of 85°. Converting to quadrant bearing form, that becomes N 85° E. Now I can project forward 600 ft along this direction using sine and cosine components to find the endpoint coordinates.

Breaking down the displacement: dx equals 600 × sin(85°) ≈ 597.00, and dy equals 600 × cos(85°) ≈ 51.54. Adding these to PI-2's position gives me the final point at approximately [2384.85, 2912.64], placing the curve's endpoint at 2500 ft and the total alignment length at 3100 ft.

Now I'll construct the alignment using these computed points. I need to organize the segments properly—the initial tangent runs 800 feet to PI-1, followed by a left-turning curve with 40° deflection, then another straight segment, and finally a second curve before reaching the end. In RoadDraft format, each segment specifies the deflection angle and distance, with any associated radius applying to the curve that follows it.

The curves are positioned so their radius applies at the start of the next leg. For the 700-foot curve segment beginning at PI-1, the 500-foot radius governs it, and similarly, the 700-foot radius for the second curve applies at its start.

I should verify the deflection angles are correctly formatted—RoadDraft accepts them as strings like '40 L' or '25°00'00" RT', which I have ready to use. Setting the current layer to align_MAIN for drawing the centerline, then creating the alignment with the specified parameters.

Looking at the alignment creation syntax, I can either supply PIs directly with their coordinates and radii, or provide legs as bearings/distances paired with radii. My approach uses the leg method: starting at [1000, 3000], moving S 80° E for 800 ft to reach the first PI, then applying the 40° left deflection on a 500 ft radius for the next 700 ft segment.

Continuing from there, I move 700 ft through to the second PI, apply a 25° right deflection on a 700 ft radius, and travel the final 600 ft to complete the alignment.

Before I can visualize this alignment, I need to create the necessary layers and set up annotation settings. Let me configure the layers with appropriate line types and weights, then establish an annotation scale to ensure measurements render at the correct sizes.

Let me first create the alignment. The description says:
- Begins at N 3000, E 1000 (so [1000, 3000] in RoadDraft coordinates)
- Station 10+00
- Runs S 80°00'00" E for 800 ft to PI-1
- Deflects 40°00'00" left on a 500 ft radius curve
- Then 700 ft to PI-2
- Deflects 25°00'00" right on a 700 ft radius curve
- Then 600 ft to end

I need to use create_alignment with legs format. Let me parse this:

First leg: bearing "S 80°00'00" E", distance 800
Second leg: deflection "40 L", radius 500, distance 700
Third leg: deflection "25 R", radius 700, distance 600

But wait, let me re-read. In RoadDraft, offset distances are positive to the RIGHT of the direction of stationing. So:
- Left side = negative offsets (since it's opposite to the direction)
- Right side = positive offsets

For a road with 11' lanes and 5' shoulders:
- From centerline to right lane edge: +11
- From right lane edge to right shoulder edge: +11+5 = +16
- From centerline to left lane edge: -11
- From left lane edge to left shoulder edge: -11-5 = -16

So the offsets array should be ["-16", "16"] for the outside edges of shoulder.

  Δy = -800 * cos(80°) = -800 * 0.1736 = -138.90

- PT-1 = PI-1 + tangent vector rotated 40° CCW
  
At PI-1 heading S 80° E (bearing 190°), turning 40° left gives new heading 230°. The tangent distance T = R*tan(20°) = 145.32 ft and the curve ends at PT-1 = [2133.16, 2515.76], matching the computed point.

From PT-1 to PI-2 along the second tangent segment, I move 700 ft at bearing 230°: Δx = 700*cos(50°) = 450.15 ft and Δy = -700*sin(50°) = -536.23 ft, placing PI-2 at [2583.31, 2363.53].
